strengths: A highly scalable and practical data construction pipeline (Clean-PR) that transforms noisy, unverified GitHub pull requests into a high-quality, verifiable repository-level training corpus.

Innovative design decisions, such as deterministic round-trip verification to convert brittle unified diffs into robust Search/Replace blocks, and augmenting PR descriptions with linked issue contents to align with real-world bug-fixing intents.

The introduction of an Agentless-aligned stepwise SFT combined with error-driven augmentation, which specifically addresses the critical challenge of 'over-editing' by teaching the model to reject irrelevant files or distractor regions.

Strong and convincing experimental results on SWE-bench Lite and Verified, showing that the 32B model can significantly outperform much larger (72B) baselines and complex agentic scaffolding by internalizing capabilities directly into the weights.

A thorough analysis of training dynamics showing that the Clean-PR training objective successfully prevents catastrophic forgetting on general coding benchmarks (HumanEval and LiveCodeBench), unlike standard diff-based training.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single base model family (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B). It remains to be shown if the training recipe is equally effective across different model sizes (e.g., 7B, 14B) or other architectures.

High computational cost for the mid-training stage (259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs), which might make it difficult for resource-constrained groups to reproduce or adapt the full multi-language training from scratch.

While the paper demonstrates strong performance under a simplified Agentless framework, it does not explore whether these internalized weight-level capabilities are complementary to more complex, multi-turn agentic scaffolding (e.g., SWE-agent or OpenHands).

strengths: Highly impressive empirical results: achieving +13.6% on SWE-bench Lite and +12.3% on Verified over the baseline instruct model, outperforming complex agentic systems (e.g., SWE-Gym) and much larger 72B parameter models.

Rigorous data-centric approach: The pipeline for converting raw, noisy GitHub PRs into high-fidelity Search/Replace blocks with round-trip bit-wise verification is extremely robust and addresses the fragility of standard git diff formats.

Well-designed intent augmentation: Linking and appending issue descriptions to raw PRs ensures the model learns the mapping from high-level natural language problem descriptions to exact multi-file edits, which closely aligns mid-training with downstream tasks.

Demonstrates positive transfer and avoids catastrophic forgetting: The paper shows that mid-training with clean Search/Replace blocks actually sharpens general coding capabilities (improving HumanEval and LiveCodeBench performance) compared to standard diff training.
Detailed ablation studies that clearly isolate the benefits of the edit format, issue-linking, multi-language training, and error-driven augmentation.
weaknesses: While the mid-training corpus spans 12 languages and multi-lingual training is shown to improve Python-only SWE-bench performance, the paper lacks explicit downstream evaluation on repository-level code editing in non-Python languages (e.g., using Multi-SWE-bench or SWE-PolyBench).

High computational cost: The 17.7B token multi-language mid-training requires a substantial amount of compute (approx. 259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs), which might limit its reproducibility for resource-constrained research groups.

Clarification is needed regarding the SFT trajectories sourced from SWE-Gym and SWE-rebench; the authors should explicitly state and confirm that there is zero overlap or leakage from these trajectories into the SWE-bench Lite and Verified evaluation sets.

strengths: Rigorous and Scalable Data Pipeline: The transformation of noisy raw GitHub PRs into verified Search/Replace blocks (via the round-trip verification in Algorithm 1) is exceptionally sound and directly addresses the brittleness of standard unified diff line numbers.

High-Quality Scale: The curation and release of a clean, multi-language corpus of 2M PRs (17.7B tokens) with linked issue contexts is a major data contribution to the open-source software engineering community.

SOTA Performance: Achieving 24.3% on SWE-bench Lite and 30.6% on SWE-bench Verified with a 32B model under a simplified, deterministic Agentless-style scaffold is impressive. It surpasses larger 72B models and systems relying on heavy agentic scaffolding.

Prevention of Catastrophic Forgetting: The paper successfully demonstrates that mid-training on structured Search/Replace blocks actually improves general coding capabilities (HumanEval +5.7%), whereas training on raw diffs degrades them.
Thorough Ablation and Analysis: Clear and well-structured ablation studies quantify the impact of the edit format, issue linking, and error-driven SFT augmentation.
weaknesses: High Computational Requirements: Mid-training a 32B model on 17.7B tokens requires massive compute resources (259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs), which severely limits replication and accessibility for researchers with limited budgets.

Lack of Cross-Model Evaluation: The proposed mid-training pipeline is only demonstrated on the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B base. Evaluating the pipeline on other model families (e.g., Llama-3-base) or smaller model scales (e.g., 7B/14B) would better prove the generalizability of the Clean-PR dataset.

Static Noise Source: The error-driven SFT augmentation relies on a static intermediate model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct) to generate distractors and negatives. It is unclear if an iterative/active learning loop using the mid-trained model itself would yield even better-aligned hard negatives.

strengths: Proposes Clean-PR, a highly rigorous and scalable data pipeline that converts raw GitHub PRs into high-quality training signals using a robust Search/Replace format and issue-linking context.

Excellent and thorough experimental evaluation, showing state-of-the-art results on SWE-bench Lite and Verified using a simplified inference scaffolding, significantly outperforming much larger models and complex agentic setups.
Thorough decontamination and semantic leakage analysis, proving that the gains are due to actual generalization rather than test-set contamination.
Comprehensive ablation studies that clearly isolate the benefits of mid-training, the Search/Replace edit format, issue augmentation, error-driven SFT, and multi-language training.
Demonstrates positive transfer (mitigating catastrophic forgetting) on standard code generation benchmarks like HumanEval and LiveCodeBench.
weaknesses: High computational requirements: Mid-training on 17.7B tokens using 32 H200 GPUs is extremely expensive and limits direct reproducibility for resource-constrained academic groups.
Complexity and scope of PRs: The dataset construction limits PRs to those modifying at most five core files, which may bias the model against massive, cross-cutting repository changes.
The evaluation focuses exclusively on the Qwen2.5-Coder model family; showing generalization to another base model family (e.g., Llama-3-Base) would strengthen the generalizability claims.

strengths: Presents Clean-PR, a massive and meticulously cleaned dataset of 2 million verified PRs (17.7B tokens) across 12 languages, representing a major resource contribution to the software engineering and code LLM community.

The data processing pipeline is highly rigorous: it converts fragile unified diffs into robust Search/Replace blocks and validates them via round-trip patch application (Algorithm 1) to eliminate formatting noise and ensure correctness.

Introduces an elegant Agentless-Aligned SFT strategy coupled with Error-Driven Augmentation, which directly tackles the critical challenge of model over-editing when presented with noisy/distractor context.

Achieves exceptional empirical results on SWE-bench Lite (+13.6%) and Verified (+12.3%) over the base model, outperforming much larger 72B parameters baselines while using a simplified inference protocol.
Exhibits positive transfer and avoids catastrophic forgetting on general coding benchmarks (HumanEval and LiveCodeBench), showing that structured editing training can sharpen general capabilities.
Includes extensive generalisation and scalability studies across different model sizes (7B), multilingual setups, and alternative agentic frameworks (OpenHands).
weaknesses: The computational requirement for mid-training (259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs) is substantial, which may limit direct reproducibility or continuous pre-training research for resource-constrained academic groups.

The data selection pipeline intentionally filters out complex, large-scale PRs modifying more than five files. Consequently, the model might remain under-supervised on broad, cross-cutting architectural refactoring tasks.

strengths: Highly impressive end-to-end results on SWE-bench (both Lite and Verified), where the proposed 32B model significantly outperforms instruct baselines and even larger 72B models under a lightweight agentless protocol.

Rigorous data construction pipeline that converts brittle unified diffs into deterministically verified Search/Replace blocks (via round-trip sandbox validation), which effectively avoids catastrophic forgetting on standard code benchmarks like HumanEval.
Exemplary decontamination protocol and semantic leakage analysis that thoroughly rule out test-set memorization or data leakage as the source of the performance gains.
Comprehensive and diverse set of evaluations, including scaling down to 7B, testing on multilingual SWE-bench, and transferring the learned capability to multi-turn agentic scaffolds (OpenHands).
A very significant artifact contribution to the open-source community by releasing a verified, multi-file, 2M PR-derived code editing dataset across 12 languages.
weaknesses: High computational requirements (259 hours on 32x H200 GPUs for the full mid-training run) which might limit the feasibility of full replication or further exploration of hyperparameter tuning for academic labs with restricted resources.
The 'at-most-five-core-files' filter used for complexity control restricts the model's exposure to large, cross-cutting repository-wide changes, which are common in very large software systems.
